query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating atomic-scale disorder metrics (e.g., configurational entropy and local strain fields) and anharmonic lattice dynamics parameters into a data‐driven machine learning model will significantly improve the prediction of low phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys for thermal-insulation applications compared to conventional averaged-property models.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy samples synthesized with near-equimolar compositions using standardized processing that results in a well-mixed, disordered solid solution.
generation.intervention: Application of a hybrid computational workflow that couples density functional theory (DFT) phonon calculations with a supervised machine learning regression model enriched with disorder-sensitive descriptors and anharmonic interaction parameters.
generation.conditions: Measurements conducted over a range of temperatures from ambient to moderately elevated temperatures, ensuring that anharmonic effects and local strain variations are appreciable; the approach is applied to HEAs within the compositional space where disorder metrics are well characterized.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale disorder (configurational entropy and local strain fields) which modulate phonon lifetimes through enhanced anharmonic scattering.
generation.mechanism: By explicitly accounting for the structural disorder and anharmonic interactions, the predictive model can capture variations in phonon scattering rates that conventional models average out, thereby providing more accurate predictions of low thermal conductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will achieve approximately a 15–20% improvement in prediction accuracy for phonon thermal conductivity and successfully identify high-entropy alloys with phonon thermal conductivity below a critical threshold set for thermal insulation applications.
generation.baseline: Traditional predictive models that use averaged compositional parameters and simplified phonon scattering treatments without incorporating disorder‐sensitive or anharmonic descriptors.
generation.boundary: The approach may be limited to HEAs whose compositional range and structural disorder are sufficiently captured by the chosen descriptors and in temperature regimes where anharmonic effects are dominant. Its performance in alloys with significant contributions from other scattering mechanisms remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of prediction improvement is not precisely known, and the model’s applicability might be compromised in HEAs where additional mechanisms (e.g., electron-phonon coupling or microstructural inhomogeneities) significantly affect the thermal transport.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of high-entropy alloy samples spanning the compositional space of interest. Utilize the new hybrid computational workflow to predict their phonon thermal conductivity and compare these predictions with those from conventional models. Then, perform experimental measurements (e.g., using time-domain thermoreflectance or laser flash analysis) of the phonon thermal conductivity over a range of temperatures.
measurements: Experimental phonon thermal conductivity values at ambient and elevated temperatures
Statistical metrics of prediction accuracy (e.g., RMSE) for both the new model and the traditional model
Identification of alloys with measured thermal conductivity below the application-specific threshold
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the new predictive approach does not demonstrate at least a 15% improvement in accuracy (as measured by a statistically significant reduction in error metrics) over the conventional model in identifying alloys with thermal conductivity below the threshold, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The CALPHAD-based HTCs

The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available.
